summary: Defines a new CoAP response code for a server to tell a client it is sending requests too fast, and should slow down. It is like HTTP's Too Many Requests.

eli5.summary: A busy shopkeeper says too many people at once, wait a bit. This gives small devices a way to say that.

questions: coap too many requests response code
subtitle: A CoAP response code that tells a client it is sending requests too fast and must wait before trying again.

tldr.problem: A CoAP server can be overloaded because one or more clients send requests faster than the server is capable or willing to handle, and the existing 5.03 code does not say the client's own request rate is the cause.
tldr.mechanism: The document registers response code 4.29, "Too Many Requests", and reuses the Max-Age option to tell the client how many seconds to wait before sending a similar request again.
tldr.outcome: Servers can now push back on individual fast clients, and clients that obey back off for the Max-Age period (60 seconds if the option is missing). The code is a Proposed Standard and has not been obsoleted.

today: RFC 8516 is a Proposed Standard and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It is the definition of CoAP response code 4.29.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
The Constrained Application Protocol (CoAP, RFC 7252) uses response codes so a server can report the result of a request. They resemble HTTP status codes, and many are shared. HTTP has a code 429 for "Too Many Requests" (RFC 6585).

RFC 8516 registers the CoAP counterpart, 4.29, with a similar purpose. It uses the Max-Age option to indicate a back-off period after which the client can try the request again. The acknowledgements note that this definition was originally part of the Publish-Subscribe Broker for CoAP document.
sections.eli5: HTTP already has a "slow down" message. CoAP, the language of tiny devices, did not, so this document adds one.

sections.title: Similar Requests and 4.29 versus 5.03
sections.content:
A server may be unable to answer one kind of request but still able to answer another, even from the same client. So the back-off period applies only to similar requests. A request is similar if it has the same method and Request-URI. Requests that belong to one series, such as a set of measurements for the server to process, can also count as similar even when their URIs differ. Because this depends on context, the application logic decides how similarity is judged.

The 4.29 code resembles 5.03 "Service Unavailable", which can also signal overload and also uses Max-Age. The difference is the cause: 4.29 says the too-frequent requests from this client are the reason for the overload. If other clients are sending requests that cannot be served, 5.03 is more appropriate.
sections.eli5: If you ask the cafeteria for the same tray again and again, you are told to wait. But if the whole cafeteria is simply swamped, everyone gets the "we are closed for a moment" sign instead.

sections.title: Server Behavior
sections.content:
If a server cannot serve a client that sends requests more often than the server is capable or willing to handle, the server SHOULD respond with 4.29. The Max-Age option gives the number of seconds after which the server assumes it is OK for the client to retry. The server can also send an action result payload to give more guidance, for example details of the overload situation.

A client may repeat a request before Max-Age has passed, either because it sent several requests before the first answer arrived or because it did not recognize the code. To slow down clients that do not recognize 4.29, the server MAY reply with a more generic error such as 5.03.

The server SHOULD rate-limit its 4.29 replies, taking its usual load-shedding policies into account. The RFC warns that any method adding per-client state to the server may be counterproductive to reducing the load.
sections.eli5: The shopkeeper says "wait a minute" and says how long. If a customer does not understand that phrase, the shopkeeper may use a plainer one. And the shopkeeper should not spend all day saying it.

sections.title: Client Behavior
sections.content:
A client that receives 4.29 SHOULD NOT send a similar request to the server before the time in the Max-Age option has passed. If the response has no Max-Age option, the client assumes the default of 60 seconds defined in RFC 7252.

A client may get 4.29 on its very first request to a server. This can happen when a proxy on the path aggregates the load of several clients, or when the client restarted recently and does not remember its recent requests.

Finally, a client should not rely on a server being able to send 4.29 in an overload situation, because an overloaded server may not be able to reply to some requests at all.
sections.eli5: When told to wait, you wait. If no time is given, count to 60. And do not expect the shopkeeper to always have time to tell you.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The security considerations of RFC 7252 apply to this code too. Replying to requests consumes server resources, so for a server under attack it may be more appropriate to drop requests without responding at all. Dropping is also likely to make well-behaving clients simply retry.

A client should trust a 4.29 reply only as far as it trusts the underlying security mechanism, such as DTLS (RFC 6347), for authentication and freshness. If the reply is not authenticated and integrity protected, an attacker can spoof it and make the client wait an extended period before trying again. Sent without encryption, the code may also leak information about the server overload situation and client traffic patterns.
sections.eli5: A fake "please wait" note could trick you into standing around for ages, so only believe notes that you know really came from the shopkeeper.

sections.title: IANA Registrations
sections.content: IANA registered response code 4.29 with the description "Too Many Requests" and RFC 8516 as the reference, in the "CoAP Response Codes" subregistry of the "Constrained RESTful Environments (CoRE) Parameters" registry. IANA also added this document as an additional reference for the Max-Age option in the "CoAP Option Numbers" subregistry.
sections.eli5: The official list of CoAP messages got one new entry, number 4.29, with this document named as its author.
